<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Poor oral health is associated with functional decline and mortality in older adults, yet causal evidence linking oral health improvement with functional independence remains limited. We simulated the effects of hypothetical reductions in oral frailty on the cumulative probability of being alive and independent in basic activities of daily living (ADLs) among older adults in Brazil.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from the EpiFloripa Aging Cohort Study of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Florianópolis, Brazil, followed from 2009 to 2023, were analysed (1,702 participants). Oral frailty was measured at waves 1–3 using a seven-item composite score (range 0–7). The primary outcome was the cumulative probability of being alive and ADL-independent through wave 5, estimated using a discrete-time survival model. Longitudinal modified treatment policies with targeted maximum-likelihood estimation simulated nine oral health improvement scenarios, accounting for time-varying confounding and censoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>336 deaths occurred during follow-up. A stepwise reduction in oral frailty increased the probability of being alive and ADL-independent by 73% (Probability Ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.48–2.02), corresponding to 15,829 additional functionally independent older adults per 100,000 individuals. Preventing edentulism with preserved masticatory function also improved the probability of being alive and ADL-independent (Probability Ratio 1.21, 95% CI 1.08–1.36). Effects on survival alone were smaller and less certain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Reducing oral frailty and preserving masticatory function increases functional independence among older adults, with smaller and uncertain effects on survival. Oral health is a modifiable determinant of healthy ageing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Reducing oral frailty improves functional independence in older Brazilians: A causal inference study of disability-free survival using longitudinal modified treatment policies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Population aging has intensified demand for data infrastructure that supports life-course, cohort, and within-person research using longitudinal surveys. However, traditional file-centric dissemination and the growing number and diversity of aging data collections have complicated secondary analysis, limiting researchers’ ability to locate comparable measures, evaluate cross-wave continuity, and assemble cross-study analytic datasets. To address these challenges, we introduced the National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal, a variable-level metadata discovery and extraction platform developed by NACDA in collaboration with Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research and Colectica.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Established in 2019, the portal integrates 17 longitudinal aging studies encompassing over 210,000 variables. Organized by concept and harmonized metadata, users can identify and extract variables across waves and studies within standardized conceptual frameworks and generate tailored documentation to support transparent, reproducible workflows. We present a use case demonstrating metadata-driven, variable-level access for longitudinal data preparation and cross-study comparison.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The portal provides concept-oriented, variable-level discovery and extraction that streamlines identification of comparable measures, supports cross-wave assessment of measurement continuity, and reduces technical and cognitive burdens associated with assembling longitudinal analytic files. The use case illustrates how variable-level access and autogenerated documentation facilitate efficient dataset construction and reproducible analysis pipelines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By shifting from file-centric dissemination to harmonized, concept-based metadata and variable-level extraction, the NACDA Portal lowers barriers to longitudinal and cross-study aging research. This approach can strengthen transparency, comparability, and reproducibility, supporting cumulative science as aging data resources continue to grow.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The National Archive of Computerized Data on Aging (NACDA) Portal: Variable-level discovery and custom metadata and data extraction for aging research

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Speaking up about quality and safety issues can protect older people and support learning in health and social care systems. In aged care, staff work in diverse roles to deliver care to residents with complex care needs. This meta-ethnography aimed to synthesise evidence on staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in long-term residential aged care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We included qualitative studies examining staff experiences of speaking up, incident reporting, and whistleblowing. Five databases were searched. The seven phases of meta-ethnography were used to translate first and second order constructs into third order constructs and a line-of-argument synthesis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirteen articles of 11 studies were synthesised to reveal four third order constructs: 1. Sensemaking a concern, 2. Organisational cultures determine how they are voiced, heard and respond to, 3. Systemic resources shape and constrain possibilities for voicing, and 4. Normalisation of poor care and loss of moral agency in organisations that respond with indifference. Raising concerns was a dynamic, recursive process encompassing phases of recognising, voicing, and organisational responding. Where quality and safety issues were normalised, individualised, or met with limited action, staff described moral distress, disengagement, and, in some cases, exit from the organisation or sector.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Raising concerns in residential aged care is a dynamic process shaped by interrelated individual, organisational and systemic factors. Speaking up interventions need to go beyond skills training to address phases of recognising care quality issues and how organisations respond when they are raised.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A meta-ethnography of staff experiences of raising concerns about quality and safety in residential aged care

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A sense of Home is an important part of wellbeing for all peoples, and there are unique dimensions to Home for Indigenous elders. Yet, there is a dearth of literature exploring the experiences and perspectives of Indigenous peoples in aged residential care (ARC) settings, and even less so from the perspectives of Indigenous elders themselves. The objective of this scoping review is to investigate and synthesise literature on Indigenous conceptualisations of Home and Home features in ARC settings from Indigenous elders’ perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research design and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review was conducted through a systematic search of qualitative research from PubMed, PsycInfo, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar databases. A framework considering Home holistically across physical, emotional, mental and spiritual domains was used to analyse findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifteen articles met the eligibility criteria for review. Indigenous elder’s spoke to several significant features of Home in ARC settings related to Cultural Home, Physical Home, Emotional/Psychological Home and Relational/Social Home.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Indigenous peoples have differential access to ARC settings as well as unique desires, attitudes and aspirations for thriving in ARC settings. They further bring embodied and rich knowledges into their environments as eminent holders of intergenerational knowledges and cultural practices. Research has demonstrated that homelike environments are favourable in ARC settings. This review advocates for aged care systems to embed culturally relevant care and home practices that prioritise relationality and Indigenous knowledge at the core of service design and delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Indigenous conceptualisations of Home in aged residential care settings: a scoping review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Person-centered care (PCC) has shaped dementia care reforms and informed innovative long-term care models such as care villages. Recreational activities are often seen as a site where PCC is enacted, yet little empirical work has examined how participation in structured activities is enabled, mediated, and constrained through everyday social, relational, and organizational dynamics. This study examines how participation in structured group activities was produced in a care village.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An ethnographic study was conducted in Canada’s first publicly funded care village, drawing on 100 hours of participant observation, 12 staff interviews, and informal resident conversations. Data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participation varied across activity types and residents’ fluctuating comfort, stamina, and readiness. For many residents, participation was not simply an individual decision, but was scaffolded through staff invitation, accessible information, relational familiarity, and individualized encouragement. It also depended on logistical and organizational conditions, including preparation, transportation, staffing coordination, and role boundaries. These findings show that participation was relationally and organizationally produced rather than simply a matter of resident preference or program design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Structured activities can support meaningful engagement when sustained by relational, logistical, and organizational work. The findings clarify how PCC commitments such as choice, autonomy, and inclusion are enacted through activity systems, while highlighting the labor-intensive conditions required for more equitable participation. These insights have implications for staffing, coordination, and activity provision in care villages and long-term care settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Beyond Attendance: Participation and Relational Work in Planned Group Recreational Activities in a Long-Term Care Village Setting

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To explore age-specific insights into how older adults understand and decide about health screening, using dementia screening as a critical case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 44 community-dwelling older adults in Singapore (ages 64–87). Six focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted. Audio recordings were transcribed, standardized into English, and verified through independent bilingual checks. Data were analyzed using a hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis grounded in Health Belief Model constructs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six main themes with twelve subthemes were identified from the analysis. Dementia understanding described participants’ general awareness of dementia and confusion between normal ageing and cognitive impairment. Risk perceptions included perceived severity and susceptibility, with many viewing dementia as an inevitable part of ageing rather than something preventable. Perceived benefits encompassed early detection, improved awareness, and protection of family members through future planning. Perceived barriers involved both practical and psychological factors, including financial cost, accessibility, fear of diagnosis, and concerns over autonomy loss. Perceived support highlighted the influence of family encouragement, community resources, and spiritual faith in motivating or discouraging screening decisions. An emergent theme of self-ageism reflected internalized beliefs that screening was unnecessary, inappropriate, or futile in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dementia screening, as a critical case, revealed how self-ageism, alongside conventional HBM constructs, shapes older adults’ screening intentions, underscoring the need for inclusive health communication for aging populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: “Not for Our Age”: Self-Ageism in Older Adults’ Dementia Screening Decision

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gratitude and savoring have great potential to support well-being in older age, but most studies on positive psychology interventions have been conducted among healthy young adults. This narrative review explored gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults, with or without dementia, including (1) the characteristics of these interventions, (2) their acceptability for older users, and (3) their effect on mental health.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scopus, PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and CINAHL were searched in December 2023 and April 2025. Studies were eligible if they examined gratitude or savoring interventions among older adults. Multi-component intervention studies were excluded. Two researchers independently screened 2423 studies and assessed methodological quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Numerical and narrative data were extracted and synthesized regarding intervention characteristics, acceptability, and effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 11 included articles, five examined gratitude, five examined savoring, and one compared both. Only one study included participants with dementia. Adherence was generally high, suggesting a good fit, but participant evaluation was lacking. Four acceptability themes were highlighted concerning the target group, setting and delivery mode, dosage, and content and tailoring. Most studies showed improved well-being and reduced psychopathology, although not consistently on all outcome measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There is initial evidence that gratitude and savoring interventions could be suitable to promote mental health among older adults with relatively preserved cognitive function. Future research should examine the need for tailoring in terms of dose, delivery method and content, and applicability to more diverse groups of older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Gratitude and savoring interventions for older adults: a narrative review

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article explores the discursive, industrial, artistic, and practical interconnections between older people, aging, and holography, arguing that their nexus mutually shapes how both concepts are culturally constituted. Methodologically, the paper utilizes a discourse and representation analysis to examine a heterogeneous corpus of actual wave-optic holography and pseudo-holographic lens-optic phantasmagorias—collectively addressed as “(quasi-)holographic” phenomena. Dissolving the boundaries between cultural fiction and industrial technology, the analysis tracks two central thematic clusters revolving around exclusion and inclusion to interrogate how older adults are integrated into techno-social futures. The paper demonstrates that while older individuals are frequently subjected to exclusionary transhumanist logics or paternalistic, resource-scarcity-driven care practices, they also emerge as active agents of inclusive technology. By analyzing cases ranging from speculative science fiction to real-world care appliances, this study maps a neglected intersection in media and aging studies. Ultimately, it introduces the concept of “geronto-futurist” interventions. These practices not only expose the marginalized position of older adults in technological imaginations but actively reshape techno-futurities. By introducing an age lens to media practices, this article contributes to broader discussions of techno-social equality, highlighting how notions of later life actively shape contemporary understandings of digitality.</jats:p>
title: From ‘Old Man Yells at Cloud’ to Geronto-Futurism: Co-Imagining Holography and Aging

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are important life-course determinants of health and may contribute to vulnerability in later life. Frailty and cognitive outcomes are important concerns in older adults, yet evidence linking ACEs to these outcomes has not been systematically synthesized. This review evaluated the associations between ACEs and frailty or cognitive outcomes in middle-aged and older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched seven databases from inception to December 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed where possible, and remaining findings were synthesized narratively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-six observational studies met the inclusion criteria. Five studies contributed to the meta-analysis of frailty outcomes and six to cognitive outcomes. ACEs were associated with higher odds of frailty (OR = 2.05, 95% CI 1.61–2.63), objective cognitive impairment (OR = 1.46, 95% CI 1.18–1.82), and subjective cognitive decline (OR = 2.04, 95% CI 1.40–2.98). Narrative synthesis revealed substantial heterogeneity in the measurement of ACEs, frailty, and cognitive outcomes across studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ACEs are associated with increased risks of frailty and adverse cognitive outcomes in later life. These findings underscore the importance of a life-course perspective in aging research and suggest that childhood adversity may be relevant to later-life risk identification and prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Adverse Childhood Experiences, Cognitive Outcomes, and Frailty in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Discourse on age-friendly communities (AFCs) calls for the meaningful inclusion of older adults as partners and contributors to community-change processes. Nevertheless, there has been very little theoretical or empirical attention as to why older adults’ involvement matters. Our study aimed to address this gap by exploring the strengths-based qualities that older adults bring as implementation actors in AFC initiatives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a secondary analysis of qualitative interview data from 23 older adults across four states in the United States about their experiences leading or partnering on the implementation of AFC initiatives (e.g., as an AFC committee chair or workgroup member). We engaged in iterative rounds of coding and analytic memo writing using abductive qualitative analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three thematic categories emerged regarding qualities that older adults bring to AFC implementation processes: (a) accumulated knowledge of aging and the community (based on prior professional and life experiences, as well as long-time residency in the community), (b) continuity of specialized skills and abilities (such as volunteer management, integrative thinking, and entrepreneurial skills), and (c) values extension and congruence with the AFC initiative (valuing older adults and the community, as well as valuing the psychosocial opportunities of participation).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We situate our findings within the broader theoretical concepts of human capital and developmental strengths. We discuss how these theoretical orientations can promote the design of more optimal opportunities for older adults’ civic contributions through AFC initiatives, with strong potential to benefit individuals and communities alike.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Human Capital and Developmental Strengths: Older Adults and the Implementation of Age-Friendly Community Initiatives

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) experience disproportionately high rates of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), yet little research examines caregiving experiences and service needs within these communities. Guided by the Sociocultural Stress and Coping Model, this study explored dementia caregiving experiences, cultural contexts, and service needs among American Indian community members, tribal health professionals, and leaders in a Northern Plains tribal community using a community-based participatory research approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In 2024, seven focus groups were conducted with 60 American Indian adults (48 community members, 12 health professionals/tribal leaders) living in the Northern Plains. Semi-structured focus groups explored caregiving experiences, cultural beliefs, and service needs. A participant background survey captured demographics and care characteristics. Qualitative data were analyzed using conceptual content analysis with iterative team-based coding.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three themes emerged across positive, negative, and service need domains. Community members emphasized cultural duty, love/reciprocity, and humor as coping mechanisms. Negative experiences included emotional and intergenerational trauma from childhood dementia exposure, and safety/supervision challenges. Critical service needs included medical guidance, community-based education, and respite services. Health professionals and tribal leaders navigated dual clinician-caregiver identities while advocating for system-level reforms. Both groups identified geographic barriers and resource scarcity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings reveal cultural strengths sustaining caregiving amid substantial systemic barriers. Effective interventions must be family-centered, community-based, and strength-focused. Healthcare systems require fundamental realignment to accommodate Indigenous epistemologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cultural Contexts of Caregiving: Exploring Alzheimer’s Disease Experiences and Service Needs Among American Indian Communities

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Shared-site intergenerational programs, which co-locate services to enable interaction across generations, have gained attention for their potential to enhance psychosocial wellbeing in later life. However, evidence explaining how and under what conditions these programs are effective remains limited. This study examined how one of Australia’s few shared-site intergenerational programs supported older adults’ psychosocial wellbeing, staff experiences, and program sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A realist evaluation was used to develop, test, and refine program theories explaining how contextual conditions interact with underlying mechanisms to generate outcomes. Data included realist interviews with residents, aged care staff, early childhood educators, and senior managers; organisational policy and procedure documents; and staff observation notes. Data were analysed using inductive, deductive, and retroductive reasoning to develop context-mechanism-outcome configurations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seven program theories were developed from twenty context–mechanism–outcome configurations. Psychosocial wellbeing was enhanced when intergenerational engagement occurred in safe and accessible environments, supported by skilled facilitation and organisational leadership, enabling participation to be experienced as meaningful and valued. These conditions activated mechanisms of belonging, reciprocity, and purpose, improving emotional wellbeing, social connection, and identity continuity. Staff experienced professional fulfilment and motivation when supported to facilitate quality engagement, while strong organisational culture contributed to sustainability. Outcomes varied where contextual supports were constrained.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Shared-site intergenerational programs function as complex relational and organisational interventions. Psychosocial benefits for residents, alongside staff wellbeing and program sustainability, depend on alignment between facilitation practices, organisational culture, and everyday institutional conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: How shared-site intergenerational programs support psychosocial wellbeing in residential aged care: a realist evaluation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Driving retirement is a significant life transition for older adults (aged 65 and older), which has been associated with negative psychosocial and health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study explores eight older adults’ plans, feelings, and support needs when stopping driving. After focus groups were conducted, participants were categorized according to Adler and Rottunda’s (2006. Older adults’ perspectives on driving cessation. Journal of Aging Studies, 20, 227–235) groupings—Proactives, Reluctant Accepters, and Resisters—to examine their nuanced perspectives. Using thematic analysis, key themes were established across groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three primary factors prompted participants across all groups to begin thinking about retiring driving, including: Medical Reasons, Safety Reasons, and Licensing Barriers. Feelings around driving retirement were predominantly negative across groups, with the exception of Acceptance; however, differences between groups were observed where Proactives tended to discuss their feelings in the past tense, whereas Resisters discussed feelings in the present tense. Using the Social Ecological Model, participants across groups highlighted the strong need to enhance support systems at interpersonal, environmental, and policy levels, with a notable absence of discussions regarding individual-level supports.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings of this study suggest that driving retirement in older adulthood may be better conceptualized as a phase-based transition, rather than categories. This phase-based approach could better inform clinicians to assist older drivers in navigating their driving retirement transition by integrating early readiness assessments, phase-specific interventions, and post-retirement emotional support. Future research should aim to further explore evidence-based interventions at the individual level that support older adults pre- and post-driving retirement to facilitate a smoother transition whilst promoting well-being.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Driving retirement in older adults: a qualitative exploration into their plans, feelings, and support needs

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease affects mostly women over 65, who make up nearly two-thirds of cases. Subjective cognitive complaints (SCC) can precede Alzheimer’s disease by years. While physical activity supports healthy aging, the long-term impact of midlife physical activity (PA) on late-life SCCs in women is limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from 4,397 participants (mean age=46.2 years at baseline; 78.7 years at SCC assessment) in the New York University Women’s Health Study (NYUWHS), a prospective cohort of 14,274 women enrolled in 1985-1991, we examined the association between midlife PA and SCC reported nearly 30 years later. PA was assessed at baseline using self-reported weekly hours of mild, moderate, and vigorous activity, converted to metabolic equivalent hours per week (MET-hours/week). Odds ratios and 95% CIs were estimated using unconditional logistic regression, adjusting for demographics and midlife and late-life health conditions. Multiple imputation and inverse probability weighting addressed missing data and potential selection bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Women in the highest tertile of total midlife PA had 20% lower odds of reporting ≥2 SCCs compared with those in the lowest tertile (OR = 0.80; 95% CI = 0.68-0.95). The inverse association was stronger among never smokers (OR = 0.68; p for interaction=0.029). The inverse association was consistent for moderate and vigorous, but not mild PA. Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses using alternative SCC definitions, exclusion criteria, and inverse probably weights.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher level of midlife PA was associated with fewer late-life SCCs, suggesting that midlife PA may be an important behavioral correlate of later-life cognitive health in women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Midlife physical activity and late-life subjective cognitive complaints in women

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cortisol dysregulation, reflective of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysregulation, has been linked to executive functioning (EF) decline. However, substantial effect-size heterogeneity across studies highlights the potential role of psychosocial moderators. We investigated whether the severity of perceived daily stressors and chronic worry moderated the relationships between baseline cortisol dysregulation and 9-year EF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Community adults (N = 1,617) completed four-day, four-times-daily salivary cortisol sampling and an eight-day interview-driven daily diary at baseline. Three cortisol metrics were computed: area under the curve (AUC), cortisol awakening response (CAR), and diurnal cortisol slope (DCS). Linear mixed models determined whether daily stressor or chronic worry severity moderated associations between baseline cortisol metrics and 9-year EF, adjusting for baseline EF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daily stressor severity significantly moderated the relationship between DCS–but not AUC or CAR–and 9-year EF (Cohen’s d = 0.113). Flatter DCS was associated with poorer EF across all stressor severity levels, although the observed numerical attenuation at higher severity was not statistically confirmed. Chronic worry severity was significantly associated with lower 9-year EF across all cortisol metrics and significantly moderated the CAR-to-EF relationship (d = –0.176). Exploratory analyses suggested that a flatter DCS was associated with worse EF at higher worry severity, but this interaction was not significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These outcomes broadly align with moderation, not mediation, suggesting that psychosocial stress and worry can amplify, rather than yield, cortisol-linked relationships with EF. Pending replication, HPA-axis circadian modulation and chronic worry severity can indicate viable targets for prevention research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Blunted Diurnal Cortisol Slope as a Risk Marker for 9-Year Executive Function Decline: Amplification by Daily Stress and Worry Severity

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Personality characteristics are recognized as early indicators of later cognitive functioning, yet existing studies have primarily focused on trait-level trends. How well these between-person differences uncover daily cognitive functioning processes remains unclear. Addressing this entails examining momentary personality states, which may accumulate over time to influence longer-term cognitive outcomes. Accordingly, this study investigates associations between personality traits and states and momentary cognitive functioning and variability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a three-week ecological momentary assessment study of middle-aged and older adults (N = 183). We used Bayesian Mixed-Effects Location Scale Models to capture contingencies between personality and momentary cognitive functioning/variability. Additionally, we used machine learning (elastic net regression) to identify profiles of personality state-cognition contingencies and individuals who exhibit stronger associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At the trait level, higher conscientiousness was associated with poorer working memory and processing speed. Higher openness was associated with better cognitive functioning and lower variability for episodic memory and processing speed. At the state level, conscientiousness was associated with better working memory performance, while neuroticism was associated with variable episodic memory functioning. Extraversion was associated with working and episodic memory functioning/variability. Finally, sociodemographic, health, and personality trait variables emerged as top predictors of individual differences in within-person associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By investigating within-person associations between personality and cognitive ability, we demonstrate that trait-level associations do not necessarily generalize to state-level ones. Profiles of top predictors of individual differences in state-level associations may be promising targets for intervention, but interventions should be tailored with between- and within-person differences in mind.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Personality trait and state associations with cognitive functioning and variability in middle-aged and older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Self-rated memory impairment is common in older age and has been related to objective cognitive decline and dementia. Recently, there has been growing interest in early-life predictors of late-life cognition, but research has been limited due to the absence of data spanning the entire lifespan. The present study investigated whether psychological health, social well-being, socioeconomic status (SES), and cognitive abilities at age 10 and 13 predicted subjective memory almost six decades later.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychological health, social well-being, SES, and cognitive abilities were measured with standardized tests and questionnaires at age 10 and 13. Subjective memory, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured with the Prospective and Retrospective Memory Questionnaire (PRMQ) and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) at age 67 (n = 625).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a longitudinal autoregressive structural equation model (SEM), higher levels of psychological health at age 13 predicted lower levels of subjective memory at age 67. This association was independent of current anxiety and depressive symptoms. The model did not provide sufficient support that social well-being, SES, cognitive ability, and school performance at age 13 predicted subjective memory at age 67. Additional analysis revealed that psychological health at age 13, but not at age 10, and anxiety symptoms at age 67 uniquely predicted subjective memory at age 67.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend prior research by showing that psychological health is a robust predictor of subjective memory. Interventions targeting early-life psychological health may help identify individuals with different prospective cognitive outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Early life predictors of subjective cognitive function in older age: Emerging longitudinal associations over six decades

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A growing body of literature suggests that self- or patient- reported health may be associated with objective health outcomes. Self-reported health could thus be a non-invasive and low-cost way of identifying who is at risk of poor health in later life. However, no prior study has systematically examined this relationship using multiple large datasets. The goal of the current study was thus to examine the extent to which self-rated health was associated with cognitive function, a distinct outcome rather than an aspect of health itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a coordinated data analysis (CDA) methodological framework, we identified 15 longitudinal datasets comprising over 140,000 participants representing 38 countries that met our analytic inclusion criteria. Our preregistered analyses tested 1) whether self-rated health was associated with cognitive function both concurrently and at longitudinal follow-up, 2) the odds of developing cognitive impairment or dementia over the course of the study, and 3) whether these associations persisted net of demographic and health covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across nearly all datasets, higher self-rated health was associated with better cognitive function (both concurrently and longitudinally) and lower odds of developing dementia, over and above the effects of chronic conditions. Age moderated some effects, such that these associations may be strongest among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The implications of these findings are discussed in terms of the predictive utility of single-item subjective health indicators on downstream health outcomes and the benefits of using CDA in aging research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations between indicators of self-rated health, cognitive function, risk of cognitive impairment, and dementia: A coordinated data analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Menopause is a heterogeneous transition that varies in timing and type, yet population-based research rarely considers how reproductive life course experiences shape menopausal outcomes. This study examines whether reproductive timing, reproductive history, and reproductive health across adolescence and adulthood are associated with menopausal status, early menopause, and surgical menopause at midlife.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from women in Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we constructed reproductive life course histories including pubertal timing, pregnancy and parity, reproductive complications, and gynecologic conditions. Menopausal outcomes at Wave VI included menopausal status, early menopause (before age 40), and surgical menopause. Survey-weighted logistic regression models estimated associations between reproductive characteristics and menopausal outcomes, adjusting for socioeconomic context and cumulative reproductive stress. Stratified analyses by pregnancy history assessed whether associations with gynecologic pathology were independent of fertility history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At Wave VI (mean age 44), 18% of women were postmenopausal. Among them, 69% reported surgical menopause and 60% experienced menopause before age 40, indicating a substantial prevalence of non-natural and early transitions. Pregnancy and parity were consistently associated with menopausal outcomes, whereas reproductive timing showed more limited associations. Gynecologic pathology was strongly associated with early and surgical menopause independent of pregnancy history.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Menopause emerges as a life course process shaped by reproductive histories and midlife reproductive health. The high prevalence of early and surgical menopause underscores the importance of examining heterogeneous pathways to menopausal timing and type in population-based research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Reproductive life course histories and menopausal outcomes at midlife: Evidence from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lifestyle activity engagement in later life may protect against dementia, but studies have often been limited to short follow-up periods and predominantly White samples. We examined activity variety and frequency as predictors of incident dementia, leveraging 15 years of linked longitudinal insurance claims data in the Baltimore Experience Corps Study (BECS).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants were 482 individuals from BECS (2006-2013) with linked insurance claims (mean age=68.2, 84% women, 95% Black/African American). Participants self-reported baseline engagement in 28 activities. We calculated the number of unique activities (activity variety) and average frequency of engagement across reported activities (activity frequency). Incident dementia (2008-2022) was ascertained from CMS and private claims using the Bynum-EM algorithm. We used Cox proportional hazards models, adjusting for age and intervention group, and tested multiple follow-up periods (5-year, 15-year).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The average baseline variety was 18.8 activities (SD = 3.3) and frequency was 13.1 days/month (SD = 3.2). For the 15-year follow-up only, higher activity variety was associated with lower risk of incident dementia (HR=.94, 95% CI: 0.89-0.99), equivalent to about a 6-month delay in diagnosis per additional activity. This association was attenuated after adjusting for additional demographics (e.g., sex, education), prevalent health conditions, and depression (HR=.96, 95% CI: 0.90-1.01). Activity frequency was not significant in any model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher activity variety, but not frequency, modestly predicted lower dementia risk over 15 years in a sample of primarily Black older adults. Findings suggest that engagement in a range of activities, rather than more frequent engagement in limited activities, may elicit greater cognitive benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Lifestyle activities and risk of incident dementia from linked insurance claims in the Baltimore Experience Corps Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Informal caregivers’ beliefs about caregiving for older adults (i.e. caregiver stigma) are associated with suicidal ideation and poor mental health. As only few studies have studied this association, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study analyzed whether caregiver stigma is associated with suicidal ideation and depression via feelings of entrapment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Canadian long-term caregivers of adults aged 60+ years (N = 175, 18-95+ years) were surveyed online with the internalized caregiver stigma scale (self-devaluing (negative) and self-affirming (positive) stereotypes, attitudes, and behaviors), about their feelings of entrapment (short entrapment scale), depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation (PHQ-9). Regression analysis with robust standard errors and causal mediation analysis with bootstrapped standard errors were conducted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Regression models indicated entrapment and negative care stigma were associated with more depressive symptoms, and entrapment with higher suicidal ideation. Significant indirect effects of positive and negative caregiver stigma components on suicidal ideation as well as depressive symptoms via entrapment were found in the causal mediation models. Additionally, positive caregiver stigma interacted with entrapment in the model for suicidal ideation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlighted that the path from negative caregiver self-stigma to a higher level of suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms seems to be rooted through increased feelings of entrapment. Conversely, the self-affirming form of caregiver stigma had a hidden protective effect for both outcomes via lower feelings of entrapment. Targeting care-related stigma may thus help reduce the danger of negative mental health outcomes among caregivers of older adults by changing their constricting perception of being trapped.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Seeing no way out: Exploring the connection between internalized caregiver stigma, entrapment, suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms among Canadian informal caregivers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the Social Ecological Model (SEM), this study aimed to examine multilevel influences on social participation among community-dwelling older adults from the perspectives of older adults and community workers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. The quantitative component included 641 community-dwelling older adults from five communities in Beijing, China. The qualitative component involved semi-structured interviews with 18 older adults and 14 community workers. Findings were integrated through an SEM-guided joint display and triangulation protocol.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older age, cognitive impairment, impairment of activities of daily living, and poor self-rated health were associated with lower social participation, whereas higher educational attainment, social support, weekly exercise, and active community encouragement were associated with higher participation. Qualitative findings identified 10 subthemes, showing that participation was also linked to interest preferences, family and peer relationships, communication and mobilization, activity design, accessibility, resource support, and policy and institutional conditions. Integrated analysis showed the clearest convergence for health- and function-related influences, while qualitative findings clarified how social support and community encouragement operated in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social participation among community-dwelling older adults appears to be associated with interrelated factors across individual, interpersonal, community, and societal levels. Efforts to support participation in later life may benefit from addressing not only functional vulnerability but also the relational, organizational, and contextual conditions that makes participation feasible in community settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Factors shaping social participation among community-dwelling older adults in China: A mixed-methods study from the perspectives of older adults and community workers

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advance care planning (ACP) is increasingly conceptualized as a proactive, communication-centered process that supports person-centered care in later life. Although prior research has focused on demographic and clinical predictors, less is known about the psychological factors that shape how individuals engage in planning. Guided by Stereotype Embodiment Theory, this study examined whether self-perceptions of aging (SPA) prospectively predict patterns of ACP engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from the Health and Retirement Study (2008–2014). A lagged longitudinal design linked baseline SPA to ACP engagement four years later among adults aged 65 and older (N = 7,618). ACP was categorized as: both formal (documentation) and informal (discussion) planning, formal-only, informal-only, or neither. Multinomial logistic regression models assessed associations between SPA and ACP patterns, adjusting for sociodemographic and health characteristics. Interaction models tested moderation by sociodemographic and health factors, and exploratory analyses examined transitions into ACP among baseline nonplanners.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More positive baseline SPA was associated with a lower likelihood of engaging in formal-only ACP relative to engaging in both formal and informal ACP. SPA was not significantly associated with informal-only ACP or with no ACP relative to comprehensive planning. Associations between SPA and ACP patterns did not vary across sociodemographic groups, although functional limitations and self-rated health modestly moderated specific contrasts. Among respondents with no prior ACP, SPA did not significantly predict transitions into planning over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings extend Stereotype Embodiment Theory to future-oriented healthcare planning and highlight SPA as a psychosocial factor associated with comprehensive ACP engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Self-perceptions of aging and advance care planning: Longitudinal evidence from the Health and Retirement Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We examined how the nationwide termination of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) Emergency Allotments (EA) affected food insufficiency among older adults aged 60 and older, a group with high rates of nutrition-sensitive disease conditions and low SNAP uptake.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using Household Pulse Survey data on older adult households with incomes below 200 percent of the federal poverty level, we applied a stacked difference-in-differences design to compare food insufficiency within three-month windows before and after EA termination.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Food insufficiency rose by 1.5 percentage points among older adult households overall and by 3.3 percentage points among older adults living alone, with no significant change among those not living alone. The difference in effects between those living alone and those not living alone was not statistically significant at conventional levels (p = 0.091). Sensitivity analyses restricting to self-identified SNAP recipients or varying the analytic window yielded consistent results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings indicate that the loss of higher SNAP benefits substantially increased food hardship among low-income older adults post-COVID, underscoring the need for adequate benefit levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Termination of SNAP Emergency Allotments increased food insufficiency among older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging is known to influence perceptual sensitivity, yet its effects on interoception across the lifespan remain poorly understood. Prior research has largely focused on single interoceptive dimensions (e.g., interoceptive sensitivity) or modalities (e.g., cardiac interoception). Moreover, most studies have assessed interoception at rest, limiting insight into how individuals track real-time changes in interoceptive state. In this study, we examined age-related differences in both interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across cardiac and respiratory modalities in healthy adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a single session, participants (N = 78; aged 18-79 years; M  age = 49.10) were assessed for: 1) interoceptive sensibility using the Multidimensional Assessment of Interoceptive Awareness (Version 2); 2) cardiac interoceptive awareness using a heartbeat tapping task under baseline and breath-holding perturbations; and 3) respiratory interoceptive awareness using an inspiratory load estimation task with varying resistance levels. Using the non-invasive interoceptive perturbations, we elicited dynamic fluctuations in interoceptive signals. Associations between age-related differences in interoceptive awareness measures were examined using linear mixed-effects models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results revealed that older age was associated with reduced cardiac interoceptive sensitivity during breath-holding, while respiratory sensitivity remained stable across ages. Additionally, interoceptive sensibility increased with age, suggesting that task-based interoceptive performance and self-reported sensibility may follow divergent aging pathways.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings demonstrate that interoceptive awareness does not decline uniformly with age but instead varies by modality and dimension. By identifying how aging differentially impacts interoceptive sensitivity and sensibility across systems, this study opens new avenues for characterizing age-related changes in interoceptive awareness and bodily regulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: How aging shapes interoception: A multimodal, multidimensional analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective views of aging (VoA) predict health outcomes, yet most studies rely on specific measures of VoA in relatively healthy samples. Referring to multidimensional (generalized and personal) and multidirectional (negative and positive) VoA constructs, we examined whether these VoA differentially predict rehabilitation outcomes among older adult patients coping with hip fracture and stroke.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred and fifty-eight geriatric rehabilitation patients (mean age=77.15, SD=6.71) reported VoA at admission while referring to negative and positive generalized (Attitudes to Aging Questionnaire, AAQ) and personal views (awareness of age-related changes, AARC). Patients' functional independence was evaluated by healthcare personnel at admission and discharge, and rehabilitation efficiency (RE) was computed to reflect functional improvement relative to potential. Path analyses tested the unique contributions of negative and positive VoA (for both generalized and personal views) while adjusting for other predictors of RE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For both generalized and personal VoA, negative views (i.e., AAQ-Losses and AARC-Losses) predicted lower RE, whereas positive views (i.e., AAQ-growth and AARC-Gains) did not show significant effects on RE. Negative views had a significantly stronger effect on RE than positive views, but only for the AAQ subscales.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the rehabilitation context, negative VoA, referring to age-related losses, appear more consequential for functional recovery than positive VoA (referring to age-related growth and gains). Findings support prioritizing interventions that identify and modify both generalized and personal attitudes, especially those focused on age-related losses, during rehabilitation to enhance functional outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The Respective Roles of Negative and Positive Views of Aging in Predicting Rehabilitation Outcomes

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Awareness of age-related change (AARC) reflects how individuals perceive age-related gains and losses, with positive perceptions consistently predicting better health and well-being. The Awareness of Age-Related Change theoretical framework has long highlighted physical and psychosocial health as distal antecedents of AARC, but their actual importance remains poorly understood. In this preregistered study, we empirically test this key model component.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We operationalize distal antecedents as 9-year trajectories in physical health (morbidity, grip strength, hearing, vision), cognitive functioning (recall, processing speed, working memory), and self-reported loneliness. We apply structural equation modeling to three-wave longitudinal data from the Berlin Aging Study II (N = 753, aged 61-81 at baseline, 49% female) and test if these trajectories predict late-life AARC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with better baseline recall and grip strength reported fewer AARC-losses, whereas those with higher baseline loneliness perceived more losses and fewer gains. Steeper declines in recall and stronger increases in morbidity were associated with heightened awareness of losses. Processing speed, working memory, hearing, and vision were not associated with AARC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results suggest several refinements of the Awareness of Age-Related Change framework: (a) within a given construct space (e.g., cognition), some dimensions (e.g., recall) are more strongly associated with perceiving age-related losses than others (e.g., processing speed), (b) long-term trajectories of recall memory and morbidity (rather than status alone) are particularly relevant for loss-focused awareness of aging, and (c) higher levels of loneliness are most consistently associated with awareness of age-related gains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Health, cognitive, and psychosocial trajectories over nearly a decade as distal antecedents of awareness of age-related change in old age

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Extensive research documents gender and racial/ethnic disparities in unpaid caregiving, defined as providing informal care to adults or children with illness, disability, or special care needs, excluding routine childcare. Yet, little is known about how the timing of caregiving entry varies across diverse groups. Despite the growing number of foreign-born Hispanics in the United States, evidence on caregiving entry among Hispanic subgroups remains scarce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used data (N=11,624) from the Health and Retirement Study (1992–2020) and the Life History Mail Survey (2017 and 2019). Using survival analysis, we estimated how the risk of entering first unpaid caregiving (lasting six months or longer) unfolds over the life course and varies by gender and racial/ethnic groups, as well as nativity among Hispanics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The likelihood of entering caregiving increased gradually with age, peaking around age 56 and declining thereafter. Women were roughly twice as likely as men to become caregivers, with the gender gap widening through midlife and persisting into old age. Differences between non-Hispanic Blacks and non-Hispanic Whites were minimal. In contrast, U.S.-born Hispanics entered caregiving earlier in the life course than non-Hispanic Whites, whereas foreign-born Hispanics showed reduced entry particularly across midlife and old age. U.S.-born Hispanics show higher entry into caregiving than foreign-born Hispanics, with differences emerging in young adulthood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings underscore persistent gender disparities in unpaid caregiving beginning early in adulthood and continuing into later life. The distinct timing patterns among Hispanic subgroups highlight the importance of considering nativity status in caregiving research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Gender and Racial/Ethnic Disparities in the Life-Course Timing of First Unpaid Caregiving: A Survival Analysis Approach

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Guided by the social compensation hypothesis, this study examined longitudinal pathways linking multidimensional social media use (SMU) to positive aspects of caregiving (PAC) among family caregivers of people with dementia. Specifically, we tested whether perceived social support (PSS) mediates the association between SMU and PAC and whether offline social network size moderates the SMU-PSS pathway.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A three-wave time-lagged panel design was conducted over six months. Data were collected from a final analytic sample of 417 family caregivers in Hong Kong and Mainland China. Path analysis within a Structural Equation Modeling framework tested a moderated mediation model in which T1 SMU predicted T3 PAC indirectly via T2 PSS, conditional on T1 offline social network size.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>T1 SMU significantly predicted T3 PAC (B = 0.141, p &lt;0.001), with a significant indirect effect through T2 PSS (B = 0.019, p = 0.027), indicating partial mediation. Offline social network size negatively moderated the SMU-PSS association (B = −0.030, p &lt;0.01). Simple slope analyses showed that the SMU-PSS relationship was significant among caregivers with smaller offline networks but non-significant among those with larger networks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings support a compensatory function of SMU: online engagement may enhance positive caregiving experiences partly by strengthening PSS, particularly for caregivers with limited offline social resources. These results inform the development of targeted digital support strategies tailored to caregivers’ baseline social networks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social media use and positive aspects of caregiving: a longitudinal test of the social compensation hypothesis

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults exhibit substantial heterogeneity in long-term care needs, yet evidence remains limited on how different patterns of home- and community-based service utilization are associated with healthcare costs across disability levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To examine the associations between patterns of home- and community-based service utilization and healthcare cost trajectories among older adults with varying levels of disability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed nationwide administrative data from Taiwan’s Long-Term Care Plan 2.0 linked with National Health Insurance claims from 2018 to 2020. Latent class analysis identified distinct service utilization patterns. Generalized estimating equations were used to estimate monthly healthcare costs over a 1-year follow-up period, stratified by disability level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five distinct service utilization patterns were identified. Integrated personal and medical care was associated with more favorable healthcare cost trajectories, particularly among older adults with moderate or severe disability, whereas more fragmented service patterns were associated with higher inpatient costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Continuous Users of Long-Term Care 2.0 Plan in Taiwan: Patterns and Health Costs Over Time

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is currently diagnosed using costly and invasive biomarkers. The Famous Faces Test (FFT) may detect (subtle) cognitive impairment earlier than standard neuropsychological tests. This review aimed to identify methodological variation across FFTs and evaluate their ability to detect early AD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases were searched. Studies were included if an FFT was used, participants were older adults or on the AD-continuum, cognitive performance-based data were reported, and the paper was a journal article or dissertation. Extracted information was clustered into stimulus characteristics, performance assessment, and participant characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>39 of 550 records met the inclusion criteria. Methodological heterogeneity was substantial. FFT performance was predominantly lower in AD-continuum individuals than in controls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recommendations for future studies using an FFT are provided, and evidence supporting its potential clinical sensitivity is reviewed. Longitudinal studies are needed to establish its utility in detecting early AD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The Famous Faces Test: A Systematic Review of Its Design and Potential for Detecting Early Alzheimer’s Disease

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Longitudinal evidence on frailty and subsequent arthritis in China is limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 4,615 adults aged ≥45 years from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (2011–2020), excluding those with baseline physician-diagnosed arthritis. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations of baseline pre-frailty and frailty with arthritis at follow-up. Sensitivity, discrimination, and exploratory subgroup analyses were performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      At follow-up, 1,219 participants (26.4%) reported arthritis. Compared with robust participants, pre-frail (OR = 1.35, 95% CI: 1.14–1.59) and frail participants (OR = 1.63, 95% CI: 1.04–2.55) had higher odds of arthritis. Findings remained directionally consistent in sensitivity analyses. Adding frailty modestly improved discrimination (AUC: 0.588 vs. 0.599; ΔAUC = 0.011;
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.017). No interaction remained significant after multiple-testing correction.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pre-frailty and frailty were associated with higher odds of arthritis after 9 years, supporting frailty as a potential longitudinal risk marker, although its incremental discriminatory value was limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Frailty and Arthritis Risk in a Population-Based Cohort: Long-Term Follow-Up and Predictive Model Evaluation
